# ==============================================================================
2+
# EXPERIMENT 2: Important Git and GitHub Commands
3+
# ==============================================================================
4+
5+
# 1. Basic Commands
6+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7+
# Initialize a new local Git repository in the current directory
8+
git init
9+
10+
# Clone an existing remote repository from GitHub to your local machine
11+
# (Replace <repository-url> with your repository link)
12+
git clone <repository-url>
13+
14+
# Check the status of working directory and staged files
15+
git status
16+
17+
# Stage all modified and new files for commit
18+
git add .
19+
20+
# Record staged snapshots to repository history with a descriptive message
21+
git commit -m "commit message"
22+
23+
# Show full commit history logs with author, date, and commit hashes
24+
git log
25+
26+
27+
# 2. Branch Commands
28+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
29+
# List all local branches in the repository (* indicates current active branch)
30+
git branch
31+
32+
# Create a new branch with the specified name
33+
git branch <branch-name>
34+
35+
# Switch to an existing branch
36+
git switch <branch-name>
37+
38+
# Create a new branch and switch to it immediately
39+
git switch -c <new-branch>
40+
41+
# Merge changes from the specified branch into the current branch
42+
git merge <branch-name>
43+
44+
45+
# 3. GitHub Remote Commands
46+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
47+
# Link the local repository to a remote GitHub repository
48+
git remote add origin <repository-url>
49+
50+
# Push the local 'main' branch to remote origin and set upstream tracking
51+
git push -u origin main
52+
53+
# Fetch and merge updates from the remote 'main' branch into local repository
54+
git pull origin main
55+
56+
# Download objects and refs from the remote repository without merging
57+
git fetch
58+
59+
60+
# 4. Undo Changes
61+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
62+
# Discard uncommitted changes in the working directory for a specific file
63+
git restore <file-name>
64+
65+
# Unstage a file from the staging area without discarding changes
66+
git restore --staged <file-name>
67+
68+
# Create a new commit that reverses the effects of a previous commit
69+
git revert <commit-id>
70+
71+
72+
# 5. Check Differences
73+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
74+
# View unstaged changes between the working directory and staging area
75+
git diff
76+
77+
# View staged changes that will be included in the next commit
78+
git diff --staged
79+
80+
# View commit history formatted as compact one-line entries
81+
git log --oneline

# ==============================================================================
2+
# EXPERIMENT 3: Create a New Repo from Command Line, Create File, and Push
3+
# ==============================================================================
4+
5+
# Step 1: Create a Project Directory (if not already created) and navigate into it
6+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7+
# mkdir my-new-project
8+
# cd my-new-project
9+
10+
# Step 2: Initialize a New Git Repository
11+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
12+
# Initialize the current directory as a Git repository
13+
git init
14+
15+
# Step 3: Create a File from the Command Line
16+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
17+
# Create a README.md file with initial content using echo
18+
echo "# My New Project" >> README.md
19+
20+
# (Optional: create another code file)
21+
# echo "print('Hello, Git!')" > app.py
22+
23+
# Step 4: Check Status and Stage the File
24+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
25+
# Verify that the new untracked file is detected
26+
git status
27+
28+
# Add the file to the staging area
29+
git add README.md
30+
# Or stage all created files:
31+
# git add .
32+
33+
# Step 5: Commit the File to Repository History
34+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
35+
# Commit the staged file with a descriptive message
36+
git commit -m "feat: initial commit with README.md"
37+
38+
# Step 6: Set the Default Branch to main
39+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
40+
# Ensure the primary branch is named 'main'
41+
git branch -M main
42+
43+
# Step 7: Link Local Repository to Remote GitHub Repository
44+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
45+
# Method A (Standard Git): Add the remote repository URL
46+
# (Replace <username> and <repo-name> with your GitHub details)
47+
git remote add origin https://github.com/<username>/<repo-name>.git
48+
49+
# Method B (Using GitHub CLI if installed):
50+
# gh repo create <repo-name> --public --source=. --remote=origin
51+
52+
# Step 8: Push Commands to Remote GitHub Repository
53+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
54+
# Note: As requested, push commands are provided in comments for reference:
55+
#
56+
# Push local 'main' branch to remote origin and set upstream tracking:
57+
# git push -u origin main
58+
#
59+
# Subsequent pushes after upstream is set:
60+
# git push

# ==============================================================================
2+
# EXPERIMENT 6: Explore Docker Commands for Content Management
3+
# ==============================================================================
4+
5+
# Command 1: Docker pull
6+
# Description: Pull an image or a repository from a registry (e.g. Docker Hub).
7+
# This command pulls the Ubuntu 16.04 image from Docker Hub to the local host.
8+
docker pull ubuntu:16.04
9+
10+
# Command 2: Docker images
11+
# Description: List images stored locally on the host.
12+
# This command displays repository name, tag, image ID, creation date, and size.
13+
docker images
14+
15+
# Command 3: Docker run
16+
# Description: Run a command in a new container.
17+
# This command creates and runs a container named "mycontainer" based on the
18+
# Ubuntu 16.04 image and attaches an interactive terminal session (/bin/bash).
19+
docker run --name mycontainer -it ubuntu:16.04 /bin/bash
20+
21+
# Command 4: Docker ps
22+
# Description: List containers.
23+
# This command lists all currently running containers along with their status and ports.
24+
docker ps
25+
26+
# (Optional: List all containers including stopped ones)
27+
# docker ps -a
28+
29+
# Command 5: Docker stop
30+
# Description: Stop one or more running containers gracefully.
31+
# This command stops the container named "mycontainer".
32+
docker stop mycontainer
33+
34+
# Command 6: Docker start
35+
# Description: Start one or more stopped containers.
36+
# This command starts the previously stopped container named "mycontainer".
37+
docker start mycontainer
38+
39+
# Command 7: Docker rm
40+
# Description: Remove one or more containers from the host.
41+
# (Note: Container must be stopped before removing, or use -f to force remove).
42+
# This command removes the container named "mycontainer".
43+
docker rm mycontainer
44+
45+
# Command 8: Docker push
46+
# Description: Push an image or a repository to a container registry (e.g. Docker Hub).
47+
# This command pushes the locally tagged image named "myimage" to Docker Hub.
48+
docker push myimage

1+
# ==============================================================================
2+
# EXPERIMENT 8: Integrate Kubernetes and Docker
3+
# ==============================================================================
4+
5+
# Step 1: Build a Docker Image
6+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7+
# Use Docker to build a Docker image of your application. You can use a Dockerfile
8+
# to specify the base image, copy the application into the container, and specify
9+
# the command to run the application.
10+
docker build -t myimage:latest .
11+
12+
# Tag the image with your Docker Hub username or container registry
13+
docker tag myimage:latest yourusername/myimage:latest
14+
15+
# Step 2: Push the Docker Image to a Registry
16+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
17+
# Push the Docker image to a container registry, such as Docker Hub or Google
18+
# Container Registry (GCR), so that it can be easily accessed by Kubernetes.
19+
docker login
20+
docker push yourusername/myimage:latest
21+
22+
# Step 3: Deploy the Docker Image to a Kubernetes Cluster
23+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
24+
# Use Kubernetes to deploy the Docker image to a cluster.
25+
# This creates a deployment that specifies the number of replicas and the image to be used:
26+
kubectl create deployment myapp --image=yourusername/myimage:latest
27+
28+
# Expose the deployment as a service to expose it to the network:
29+
kubectl expose deployment myapp --type=NodePort --port=80
30+
31+
# Step 4: Monitor and Manage the Containers
32+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
33+
# List running pods and verify the deployment status
34+
kubectl get pods
35+
kubectl get deployments
36+
kubectl get services
37+
38+
# Scale the number of replicas up or down
39+
kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=3
40+
41+
# Update the image running in the deployment (rolling update)
42+
kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=yourusername/myimage:v2
43+
44+
# Check rollout status
45+
kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp
46+
47+
# Step 5: Continuously Integrate and Deploy Changes (CI/CD)
48+
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
49+
# Use a continuous integration and deployment pipeline to automatically build,
50+
# push, and deploy changes to the Docker image and the Kubernetes cluster.
